metadata.title: Predicting cross-national sex differences in large-scale assessments of students' reading literacy, mathematics, and science achievement: Evidence from PIRLS and TIMSS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The manuscript uses PIRLS and TIMSS achievement outcomes to derive cross-national sex differences and then regresses those sex-difference indicators on country-level macro indicators (e.g., GDP per capita, gender equality indices, and education spending). The provided excerpt does not report whether student-level sampling weights or replicate weights from the PIRLS/TIMSS microdata were applied, nor does it name any weight variables. Because the analysis is described as country-level regression on standardized sex differences (rather than a student-level ML pipeline), the appropriate weighting approach would typically be to use the ILSA-provided sampling weights when estimating sex-difference effects from student data and to propagate uncertainty when aggregating to country-level effects. The excerpt does not specify this, so readers should treat the weighting and variance estimation details as not reported in the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The excerpt does not describe how missing data were handled in the PIRLS/TIMSS student-level analyses used to compute sex differences, nor does it specify the missing-data strategy for any derived indicators. This is a reporting gap because PV-based achievement measures in PIRLS/TIMSS typically require explicit documentation of PV handling and missingness treatment to ensure reproducibility and correct uncertainty quantification.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt indicates that the authors analyze multiple PIRLS and TIMSS cohorts and then compute standardized sex differences for reading literacy, mathematics, and science at grade four and grade eight, followed by regressions on country-level macro indicators. However, it does not specify which countries were included, which PIRLS/TIMSS cycles correspond to which grades, or any student-level inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., grade restrictions, valid response criteria, or missingness exclusions). The excerpt also mentions a robustness reanalysis using the bottom and top 25% of performers selected by the first plausible value, but it does not provide the exact filtering thresholds or the full set of countries.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized single regression weights: GGI β = 0.23; GPI β = 0.27; GDP per capita β = 0.08; GET β = −0.07. (p-values indicated in figure note; exact p-values not provided in excerpt.)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS reading literacy data for grade 4 across cohorts, the study leveraged Gender Gap Index (GGI), Gender Parity Index (GPI), GDP per capita, and education spending to predict standardized sex differences, finding that girls’ reading advantages were larger in countries with higher gender equality (GGI β = 0.23; GPI β = 0.27) while GDP per capita and education spending showed no meaningful associations (GDP β = 0.08; GET β = −0.07). This indicates that cross-national gender equality—rather than overall education expenditure or national prosperity—may be a key macro-context for the size of girls’ reading literacy advantages, though the excerpt does not report student-level weighting/PV and thus uncertainty propagation cannot be verified.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized single regression weights: GDP per capita β = −0.39; GEP β = −0.39; GET β = −0.32; GGI β = −0.39; Gini Index β = 0.16; GPI β = 0.04.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS mathematics data for grade 4 across cohorts, the study leveraged GDP per capita, gender equality in health/education/economy/politics (GEP), education spending per primary student (GET), and the Gender Gap Index (GGI) to predict standardized sex differences, finding that boys’ mathematics advantages were larger in more prosperous and more gender-equal societies (GDP β = −0.39; GEP β = −0.39; GET β = −0.32; GGI β = −0.39) with a small positive association for the Gini Index (β = 0.16) and no meaningful effect for the Gender Parity Index (GPI β = 0.04). This indicates that macro-level prosperity and gender equality may amplify boys’ relative mathematics performance at earlier grades, suggesting that equity-oriented policy should consider how gender-equality contexts interact with mathematics participation and learning opportunities.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized single regression weights: GET β = −0.25; GES β = −0.12; GDP per capita β = 0.12; GPI β = 0.14; GGI β = −0.12; Gini Index β = −0.03.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS mathematics data for grade 8 across cohorts, the study leveraged education spending per secondary student (GES/GET) and national prosperity and gender indicators to predict standardized sex differences, finding that larger educational investment was linked to larger boys’ mathematics advantages (GET β = −0.25; GES β = −0.12) while GDP per capita and GPI showed small positive effects (GDP β = 0.12; GPI β = 0.14) and GGI showed a small negative effect (β = −0.12), with the Gini Index showing no meaningful effect (β = −0.03). This indicates that at later primary-to-lower-secondary transition ages, education spending may be more strongly associated with the gender gap in mathematics than prosperity alone, implying that how investment is targeted (e.g., gender-responsive pedagogy) may matter for reducing or reshaping gender differences.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized single regression weights: GDP per capita β = −0.36; GEP β = −0.31; GET β = −0.11 (reported as not meaningful for GEP/GPI range −0.07 to −0.01); GGI β = −0.23; Gini Index β = 0.20; GPI not meaningful (β range −0.07 to −0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS science data for grade 4 across cohorts, the study leveraged GDP per capita, gender equality in health/education/economy/politics (GEP), education spending per primary student (GET), the Gender Gap Index (GGI), and the Gini Index to predict standardized sex differences, finding medium-sized negative effects of GDP per capita and GEP on boys’ relative science performance (GDP β = −0.36; GEP β = −0.31) and a small positive effect of the Gini Index (β = 0.20), alongside a meaningful effect of GGI (β = −0.23). This indicates that macro prosperity and gender-equality contexts are associated with larger boys’ science advantages at grade four, suggesting that science equity interventions may need to be sensitive to national gender-equality and inequality environments.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized single regression weights: GDP per capita β = 0.31; Gini Index β = 0.24; GET β = −0.11; GEP β = −0.07; GGI β = −0.06; GPI β = −0.08.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS science data for grade 8 across cohorts, the study leveraged GDP per capita, the Gini Index, and education spending indicators to predict standardized sex differences, finding that GDP per capita and the Gini Index were positively associated with smaller boys’ science advantages (GDP β = 0.31; Gini β = 0.24) while education spending showed small negative effects (GET β = −0.11; GEP β = −0.07) and GGI/GPI were unrelated (GGI β = −0.06; GPI β = −0.08). This indicates that the macro-context correlates of gender gaps in science shift with age, implying that policy levers for science equity may differ between grade four and grade eight.

data.outcome_summary: The study examines cross-national sex differences in PIRLS reading literacy and TIMSS mathematics and science across multiple cohorts, focusing on grade four and grade eight. It then relates standardized sex-difference indicators to country-level macro indicators of prosperity, education investment, and gender (in-)equality (e.g., GDP per capita, GGI, GPI, GEP, GET/GES, and the Gini Index). The reported results show a highly consistent pattern of girls’ advantages in reading literacy across countries, with the size of the advantage linked mainly to gender equality indices (GGI β = 0.23; GPI β = 0.27) and not to GDP per capita or education spending. For mathematics and science, sex differences are smaller on average but vary meaningfully by country: boys’ advantages in grade four are associated with prosperity and education investment, while grade eight patterns are more mixed and appear more sensitive to education spending and economic equality. Limitations include the absence of reported student-level weighting/PV and missing-data handling details in the provided excerpt, and the fact that the analysis is correlational rather than causal.
